job.style: a passage that starts from a common wrong idea and corrects it

passage: Many people mistakenly believe that soil is simply powdered rock, but it is actually a complex mixture of weathered rock particles, decaying organic matter, air, and water. This formation process is incredibly slow, taking hundreds of years to create just a few centimeters of topsoil, rather than happening overnight after a rainstorm. The soil profile consists of distinct layers, and the topsoil is the most fertile because it is rich in humus and nutrients, unlike the deeper layers near the bedrock. Furthermore, soil is not a solid, airless block; it contains tiny spaces between particles that hold both air and water. The rate at which water passes through these spaces, known as percolation, varies by soil type. Sandy soil has large particles and a high percolation rate, meaning water drains through it very quickly, whereas clay has smaller particles that hold water tightly. Finally, plants are vital for the environment because their roots bind the soil together, acting as a natural shield against erosion. Without this protective cover, wind and water can easily wash away the fertile top layer, which is a process that affects both wild landscapes and human-inhabited agricultural fields alike.

items.evidence: The soil profile consists of distinct layers, and the topsoil is the most fertile because it is rich in humus and nutrients, unlike the deeper layers near the bedrock.
items.q: Meena wants the most fertile soil for her pot plants. Which layer should she dig out?
options: The top layer, full of humus
The deepest layer, close to the bedrock
Any layer, since all layers are alike
The lowest layer, made of soft mud
items.explain: Topsoil is most fertile because it is rich in humus and nutrients, unlike deeper layers.

wrong.why: thinks deeper soil is more fertile
ignores that the profile has distinct layers
thinks the lowest layer is soft mud

items.evidence: Furthermore, soil is not a solid, airless block; it contains tiny spaces between particles that hold both air and water.
items.q: A dry lump of soil is dropped into water and bubbles rise. Where do the bubbles come from?
options: Air trapped in tiny spaces between particles
Rock powder dissolving, since soil is only rock
The water, since solid soil holds no air
Roots breaking the rocks inside the soil
items.explain: Soil is not an airless block; tiny spaces between its particles hold air.

wrong.why: thinks soil is just powdered rock
thinks soil is solid with no air
thinks roots break rocks into soil

items.evidence: Sandy soil has large particles and a high percolation rate, meaning water drains through it very quickly, whereas clay has smaller particles that hold water tightly.
items.q: Equal amounts of water are poured on sandy soil and clay soil. What will happen?
options: It drains faster through the sandy soil
It drains faster through the clay soil
It drains at the same speed through both
It stays longest in the sandy soil
items.explain: Sand has large particles and high percolation, so water drains through it quickly; clay holds water.

wrong.why: thinks clay particles are larger than sand
misses that percolation varies by soil type
thinks high percolation means holding water

items.evidence: Without this protective cover, wind and water can easily wash away the fertile top layer, which is a process that affects both wild landscapes and human-inhabited agricultural fields alike.
items.q: A farmer clears every plant from his field. What will most likely happen to its topsoil?
options: It is carried off by wind and water
It stays safe, since people farm there
It erodes less, since roots stop breaking it
It forms again after the next heavy rain
items.explain: Roots bind soil; without plant cover, wind and water wash away topsoil, even on farms.

wrong.why: thinks erosion happens only where no people live
thinks plants cause erosion by breaking soil
thinks soil forms quickly after rain
